situation:
You are the general manager of DUNMORE LAUNDROMATS, nine self-service stores the same family has run for three generations. The owner (judge) has asked you to recommend whether the company should sign the weekly linen contract a hotel group has offered, or spend the same money on networked meters for its machines.

The hotel group wants the large-format washers every weekday morning. Since the founder's day the stores have held those machines free on weekday mornings for a nearby senior housing complex, a written commitment the neighborhood knows by name. Nobody at the company can say how many of those reserved hours are actually used, because all nine stores still count loads on paper.

One course is to sign the hotel contract. It brings steady weekly revenue into a business whose walk-in traffic has been flat for years, and it takes the reserved morning hours from the senior housing complex, breaking a commitment made in writing by a grandfather whose name is still on the door.

The other course is to spend the money on networked meters instead, which would finally show which machine hours are free and which are not. The meters return nothing that shows on a statement, and the hotel group has said it will place the contract elsewhere this quarter. The owner (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
